course_name: Know Your Leadership Pattern Under Pressure

episodes.episode_title: The importance of purpose: An interview with Acha Leke
episodes.the_idea: Acha Leke, born in Cameroon and now chairman of McKinsey's Africa region, tells on himself. When he was a manager who was not confident about his own presentation skills, his default under pressure was to hand the steering-committee presentation to an analyst or associate, and to tell his team a flattering story about giving them room to grow. The real reason was fear. It changed when someone told him flatly, 'you'll never get better if you don't practice,' so he took the next one himself, felt he did badly, and did it again. His line is that self-awareness is only step one; step two is being willing to work on the fear, including with coaches or a therapist. That is the course concept, seeing your own pattern under pressure and doing something about it, with the polish taken off. Note: this is McKinsey's own edited transcript of a live interview, published as text rather than as an audio episode, so the duration is a spoken-length estimate.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: The three questions draw from a few specific moments, not the whole interview. First, the public-speaking story near the end: how Leke used to hand presentations to the analyst or associate, the reason he gave his team, the real reason underneath, the one line of feedback that changed it, and the two-step move he names for handling a fear like that. Second, his rule about risk from early on, 'take the risk but manage the downside,' and the specific downside he decided he could live with when he moved to Africa. Third, the burnout story: the simple goal he set for his three months off, and what he chose to tell his clients. You can skip the sections on purpose, network building, and being a good protege.

questions.question: For years Leke let the analyst or associate on his team give the steering-committee presentation. What reason did he give his team, what was the real reason, and what single piece of feedback made him start presenting himself?

Leke names a two-step move: first recognize and accept the fear, then be willing to work on it, sometimes with a coach or therapist. Name one task you quietly route around under pressure, the tidy reason you give for it, and the first rep you would take to face it.

Leke's rule is 'take the risk but manage the downside' -- he reasoned that if Africa did not work out he could return to the US. Name a decision in your work where the downside is not reversible, so 'manage the downside' would give you false comfort.

episodes.episode_title: Face Uncertainty and Take Action: Lessons from a Blind Sailor's Pacific Crossing
episodes.listening_range: The full episode runs about 36 minutes. The transcript file holds only the crisis section assigned to learners, from Hiro's decision to sail the Pacific through the whale collision, the 11 hours in the life raft, and how he stayed calm, about 12 minutes of listening. The episode page carries no timecodes, so that figure is estimated from speech rate; the spoken start and end lines are noted at the top of the file.
episodes.the_idea: Hiro Iwamoto is the first totally blind person to sail across the Pacific. On an earlier attempt his boat hit a whale and sank, and he spent 11 hours in a life raft in five-metre waves. What makes this a course piece is the contrast he draws inside his own head. The night before, when nothing had gone wrong yet, he lay awake running every future disaster -- what if the waves break the boat, what if the raft does not inflate -- until his teeth shook. When the boat actually sank, he was calm, because he had shifted out of the future and into the present, saying 'arigato' to the boat and living now. His partner panicked; he did not. Same event, two default reactions under pressure, told from outside the leadership world. Worth noting: the calm was not the whole story, because they lived partly on an emergency bag, packed in advance, holding a GPS and a satellite phone.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: All three questions come from the crisis stretch saved in the transcript file. Focus on the contrast Hiro draws between the night before the whale hit, when he lay awake running through everything that could go wrong until his teeth shook, and the moment the boat actually sank, when he says he was 'very, very calm.' Pay attention to what he says pulled him out of the fear: the message from his late uncle, saying 'arigato' to the boat, and living in the present instead of the future. Note that his partner Shinbo was in a panic while Hiro stayed calm, and that they survived in part because of an emergency bag, packed in advance, that held a GPS and a satellite phone. You do not need the rest of the episode.

questions.question: Hiro says he was 'very, very calm' when the boat sank, but not the night before, when his teeth were shaking. What was he doing in his head the night before, and what exactly does he say shifted him out of it in the moment?

Hiro contrasts himself, calm and 'living now,' with his partner Shinbo, who was in a panic at the same moment. Name your own default when pressure spikes -- do you spin forward into what-ifs like Hiro the night before, or something else -- and one cue you could use to come back to the present.

Hiro's lesson is to stop running the what-ifs and 'be now.' But he and Shinbo survived only because they had already packed a GPS and satellite phone for exactly those what-ifs. Name a moment in your work where running the disaster scenarios ahead of time matters more than staying present, so 'be now' would be the wrong advice.

episodes.listening_range: The full episode runs about 55 minutes. The transcript file holds only the first stretch, where the hosts weigh whether the Myers-Briggs measures anything real, roughly the first 22 minutes, ending where they turn to the history of who invented it. The page has no timecodes, so that figure is estimated from speech rate; the spoken start and end lines are noted at the top of the file.
episodes.the_idea: This course asks people to map their personality blueprint and their pattern under pressure. This episode is the counter-case, and it is funny about it. Aubrey Gordon and Michael Hobbes take apart the Myers-Briggs, the test the whole personality-typing habit rests on. The core of the challenge is the Forer effect, shown in a 1949 experiment where a psychologist gave every student the same profile, lifted from an astrology magazine, and they rated it 4.3 out of 5; people rate a test as more valid when the description flatters them. And the test does not hold up: it claims your type is innate and permanent, yet 39 to 76 percent of people get a different result after five weeks, and only the introversion-extraversion scale matches other instruments. The honest twist is that the hosts still think the framework can be a constructive, non-judgmental way to talk about differences. Useful story, no science under it. That tension is the point for a course built on self-typing.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: The three questions come from the first stretch of the episode, saved in the transcript file, where the hosts argue about whether the Myers-Briggs measures anything real. Focus on three things. First, the Forer effect, also called the Barnum effect: the 1949 experiment by Bertram Forer, where every student got the same profile, lifted from an astrology magazine, and rated it 4.3 out of 5, plus the finding that people rate a test as more valid when the description is favorable. Second, the reliability problem: the claim that your type is innate and never changes, against the finding that 39 to 76 percent of people get a different result after five weeks, and that only the introversion-extraversion scale tracks with other instruments. Third, the contrast between the Big Five, validated by many teams over decades, and the Myers-Briggs, a self-report popularization of one of Jung's theories. You do not need the second half, the history of Katharine and Isabel Briggs.

questions.question: In the 1949 Forer experiment the hosts describe, what did every student actually receive, where had that profile come from, and what average accuracy score out of 5 did the students give it?

The hosts note the Myers-Briggs is 'designed not to hurt your feelings,' unlike the Big Five, which measures neuroticism, and that people rate flattering descriptions as more accurate. Name one label or category your team uses that only ever flatters, and one uncomfortable measure that would tell you more.

Michael still calls the Myers-Briggs 'mostly a force for good' as a constructive way to talk about differences, even with no science under it. Aubrey's own team turned it into cliques and 'we're not hiring another persuader.' Name a decision in your work where an unproven personality label would do real harm, so the 'it's harmless and constructive' defense would not hold.
